title: Pressure Points for Headache: 6 Points and a 5-Minute Routine — cv.cm
description: Six pressure points for tension headaches with exact locations, a timed 5-minute routine, what the evidence shows, and headache warning signs that need a doctor.
h1: Which pressure points help with a headache?
answer: For a tension-type headache, the most used pressure points are `GB20` under the skull at the back of the head, Taiyang at the temples, Yintang between the eyebrows, `BL2` at the inner ends of the eyebrows, `LI4` on the hand and `GB21` on top of the shoulders. Press each for 30 to 60 seconds, firm but not painful. Evidence is limited, and a sudden or severe headache needs a doctor.

sections.h: Which headaches this may help, and which need a doctor
body: Pressure points and self-massage are most often used for tension-type headaches. These are the most common headaches. The NHS describes them as pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, or a feeling of pressure or a tight band around the head. The area may feel tender to touch, and you can usually carry on with daily activities. Stress, poor sleep, long hours at a screen and tight neck and shoulder muscles often go with them. The NHS lists relaxing activities, including massage, among the things that can help.

ul: May help: tension-type headache, a tight neck and shoulders after desk work, eye strain headaches.

Not a treatment: migraine. Some people with migraine find gentle pressure or a cool cloth on the forehead soothing, but acupressure is not a migraine treatment and the studies are small. Follow the plan you have agreed with your doctor.
Needs a doctor: a new pattern of headaches, headaches several times a week, headaches that wake you up, or any warning sign listed in the safety section below.

body: If you take painkillers for headaches on many days each month, the painkillers themselves can cause more headaches. A doctor or pharmacist can help with this.

Locations follow the WHO Standard Acupuncture Point Locations (2008). Taiyang is a traditional extra point outside that list. A cun is a body-relative unit: 1 cun is about the width of your thumb at the knuckle. Use both sides unless noted.

body: Aim for 4 to 6 on a 1 to 10 pressure scale: firm but not painful. A dull ache that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning or tingling pain means stop and use less pressure. The face and temples need light to medium pressure only: the skin is thin and the bone is close.
Tension headaches often come with tight muscles at the back of the neck and the top of the shoulders. Gentle massage of those muscles fits well with the points above.

ol: Skull base: place your fingertips along the bottom edge of the skull at the back. Make small circles, moving outward from the middle to behind the ears. Keep off the bony middle of the spine.

Back of the neck: with one hand, hold the muscles on both sides of the back of the neck between your fingers and the heel of the hand. Squeeze gently, release, and move down a little. Repeat from the skull to the base of the neck.
Top of the shoulder: with the opposite hand, squeeze and lift the muscle on top of the shoulder, then release. Work from the neck out to the shoulder tip.
Temples: place the flat fingertips on the temples and make slow circles, light to medium pressure.
Forehead: with the fingertips, stroke slowly from the middle of the forehead out to the temples.

body.note: Never press or massage the front or sides of the throat. The large blood vessels of the neck run there. Work only on the back of the neck and the top of the shoulders.

body: Sit in a chair with your feet flat and your back supported. Dim the screen or close your eyes where you can. To time each step, you can use a timer, for example cv.cm's countdown.

What to do

Both thumbs under the skull base, press upward and hold
Squeeze down the back of the neck, from skull to base
Press or squeeze the top of each shoulder
Press up under the inner brows, then small circles between the brows at `GV29`
Squeeze the web of each hand

body: After the routine, drink some water, look away from the screen, and stand up for a minute. If you get tension headaches often, short breaks during the day help more than one long session.

The research on pressure points for headache is small. A 2010 randomised trial in Taiwan compared one month of acupressure with one month of a muscle relaxant drug in 28 people with chronic headache. The acupressure group reported lower pain scores after treatment and at six months. Points such as `BL2` and `GB20` were among those used. With only 14 people in each group, this is an encouraging small study, not proof.

NCCIH, the US government research centre for complementary health, says acupuncture with needles may help relieve headache pain, but much of the benefit may come from expectation and other non-specific effects. It also says only limited evidence from two small studies suggests massage may help migraine. Acupressure has been studied far less than needles.

In short: pressing points and massaging the neck is low-risk and many people find it eases tension. It is reasonable to try for tension-type headaches. Do not expect it to stop a migraine, and do not use it to delay care for a headache that worries you.

sections.h: Safety: when to stop and when to get help
body: Stop if pressing makes the headache worse, causes sharp pain, or causes numbness or tingling in the face, arm or hand. Do not press over broken skin, a fresh bruise or a recent head or neck injury. If you are pregnant, ask your midwife or doctor first; traditional advice avoids firm pressure on `LI4` and `GB21` in pregnancy.

body.note: Call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department if a headache comes on suddenly and is extremely painful (the worst ever), follows a head injury, or comes with: a fever and stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when you press a glass on it, a seizure, numbness or weakness in the face or body, trouble speaking, walking or remembering, confusion or drowsiness, or loss of vision.

body: Get an urgent appointment with a doctor if a headache comes with vision problems, is set off or made worse by coughing, sneezing, bending or exercise, comes with vomiting, or comes with jaw pain when eating or a sore, tender scalp. These signs are based on NHS guidance.

sections.h: Common mistakes and how to fix them

ul: Pressing the temples hard: the bone is thin there and hard pressure can add to the ache. Use light, slow circles.
Digging into the middle of the neck: stay in the hollows beside the spine at `GB20`, never on the spine itself.
Pushing down toward the eye at `BL2`: always press upward against the brow bone.
Doing it once when the pain is bad: short daily breaks for the neck and shoulders are more useful for frequent tension headaches.
Soreness the next day: halve the pressure and the time.

faq.q: Where is the pressure point for a headache on the hand?
faq.a: It is Hegu (`LI4`), on the back of the hand next to the middle of the index-finger bone, on the thumb side. Squeeze it between your thumb on top and your index finger under the palm for 30 to 60 seconds.

faq.q: How long does it take for pressure points to relieve a headache?
faq.a: There is no fixed time, and pressure points do not always help. Try a 5-minute routine; if the headache is unchanged, use the treatment you normally use and rest.

faq.q: Can pressure points help a migraine?
faq.a: Acupressure is not a migraine treatment, and the studies are small. Some people find gentle pressure soothing during an attack, but follow the plan from your doctor.

faq.q: Is it safe to massage your temples?
faq.a: Yes, with light to medium pressure and slow circles. Stop if it makes the pain sharper, and see a doctor if you have a tender scalp or jaw pain when eating with your headache.

faq.q: Why does the back of my head hurt when I press it?
faq.a: The muscles under the skull base are often tight and tender with tension headaches, so a dull ache when pressing is common. A headache with a stiff neck and fever, or after a fall or injury, needs urgent medical care.
